translation: 1. The world of the soul's experience: knowledge in the direct perception of its separate form.
2. The world of the experience of the cessation of the soul's own knowing, free of the distinctions of own form and of subtle notion.
3. The world of the experience of knowledge in the direct perception of the true form of the pure soul, in the awareness and inherence of full knowing as pervading and pervaded.
4. The world of the experience of direct perception of pure knowledge, in the dissolution and rising of the tattvas and the tattvic.
5. The world of the experience beyond pure knowledge, pervading and pervaded, in the dissolution and rising of the tattvas and the tattvic.
6. The world of the experience whose aim is freedom from the soul's own knowing, in the transcendent light of knowledge, fully pervading and pervaded.
7. The world of the experience whose aim is the yoga of the light of consciousness beyond fullness.
8. The world of the cessation of latent impressions in transcendent jnana-yoga.
9. The world of the experience of jnana-yoga, the excellence of the yoga of the transcendent light of consciousness.
10. The world beyond the enjoyment of experiential knowledge, in the cessation of the latent impressions of jnana-yoga.
11. The world of the pure state beyond waking, the experience of pervading and pervaded in the direct realization of own form, beyond the enjoyment of jnana-yoga.
12. The world of the experience of the nature of the joy of consciousness alone, in the transcendent fullness of consciousness.
13. The world of the own form of joy, the form of Being, not other than the transcendent fullness of consciousness.
14. The world of the experience of the form of joy, the own form of Being, in the transcendent fullness of consciousness and bliss.
15. The world of the experience of the direct realization of Siva in the undivided oneness of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidananda).
16. The world beyond the joy of oneness with Siva.
To expand this further would make it grow without end.
Thiru Chitrambalam.
Here ends the Explanation of the Meaning of the True Word "Ulagelam".
commentary: The last sixteen worlds trace the end of the ascent. The soul sees itself as separate; its own knowing ceases; the tattvas dissolve and arise before pure knowledge. Then come the light of consciousness, the end of latent impressions and the pure state beyond waking. Last are joy, Being, the direct realization of Siva in undivided oneness, and a world beyond even the joy of that oneness.

So the one word Ulagelam holds everything: the tattvas and their products, the worlds of the gods, the liberations of every school and practice, and worlds beyond all causes, up to bliss in oneness with Siva. Vallalar says the list could grow without end. The God who spoke this word in the Chit Sabhai is the One he came to name Arut Perum Jothi, open to every soul.

sections.title: The Commentary on the Word Tamil

translation: The Commentary Given on the Word "Tamil"
Thiru Chitrambalam.
commentary: Vallalar reads the word Tamil sound by sound and finds in it the whole way of the soul to God. The word has five sounds. He gives each its place: the Lord, the soul, and the supports that carry them. Then he draws the meaning together: the soul, freed from the darkness of impurity, experiences Arut Perum Jothi; and the Tamil language itself gives the experience of pure Sivam most easily. He writes in the technical language of the Saiva teaching, which he here calls Suddha Siddhanta.

sections.title: The Five Units of the Word

tamil: தமிழ் என்பது த்-அ-ம்-இ-ழ் என்னும் ஐந்து அலகு நிலையுடைத்து. த், ம், ழ்: ஜடசித்கலை. அ, இ: சித்கலை.
translation: The word Tamil has five units (alaku): t-a-m-i-ḻ. T, m and ḻ are jaṭacitkalai, powers in which the inert and consciousness are joined. A and i are citkalai, powers of consciousness.
commentary: Written out, the word Tamil has five units: three bare consonants, t, m and ḻ (the Tamil sound often written "zh"), and two vowels, a and i. Tamil grammar calls a vowel uyir, "life", and a consonant mey, "body": a consonant cannot sound without a vowel, as a body cannot live without the soul. Vallalar builds on this. The vowels are pure powers of consciousness (citkalai). The consonants are jaṭacitkalai, where the inert (jaṭam) and consciousness meet, as in a body that carries a soul. Kalai here means a power or ray of a reality.

sections.title: The Vowels a and I

tamil: அ அகண்டாகார சித்தை விளக்கும் ஓங்கார பஞ்சாக்கரத்துள் பதிநிலை அக்கரமாம்.
இ பதியை விட்டு நீங்காத சித்தை விளக்கும் வியவகாரத்தால் அனந்தாகார வியஷ்டி பேதங் காட்டும் ஜீவசித்கலை அக்கரமாம்.
translation: A is the letter of the station of Pati, the Lord, among the five letters of Omkara: it makes manifest consciousness (cit) whose form is undivided.

I is the letter of jīvacitkalai, the conscious power of the individual soul: it makes manifest the consciousness that never leaves Pati, and by its working it shows the distinctions of individual beings in endless forms.
commentary: Omkara, the sacred syllable Om, is counted as five letters: a, u, m, bindu and nāda. Its first letter, a, stands for Pati, the Lord, as consciousness without division. I stands for the individual soul (jīvaṉ). Its consciousness never departs from the Lord, yet in its working it appears as countless separate beings. So every living being carries a consciousness that has never left the Lord. This is the ground on which Vallalar asks compassion for every life (Jeevakarunyam).

sections.title: The Three Consonants

tamil: பதி சிதாத்ம கலைகளுக் காதாரமாகி உயிரினுக்குடலையொத்துக் குறிக்கப்படும் த், ம், ழ் எழுத்துக்களுக் குரை:
translation: The commentary on the letters t, m and ḻ, which are the support of the powers (kalai) of Pati and of the conscious soul (citātmā), and are marked out as being like the body to the life (uyir):
T is the seventh consonant;
m is the tenth;
ḻ, the fifteenth, is the special letter (ciṟappiyal akkaram) of natural truth (iyaṟkai uṇmai).
commentary: The three consonants carry the two conscious powers, of the Lord (a) and of the soul (i), as a body carries life. Vallalar fixes their places in the order of the eighteen Tamil consonants: k, ṅ, c, ñ, ṭ, ṇ, t, n, p, m, y, r, l, v, ḻ, ḷ, ṟ, ṉ. T is the seventh, m the tenth, ḻ the fifteenth. The numbers matter: below, the seventh place meets the seventh of the ten stages of the soul's way, and the fifteenth the number that closes a lunar fortnight. Tamil grammar calls ḻ, ṟ and ṉ the special letters (ciṟappeḻuttu) of Tamil, since they belong to it alone.

sections.title: Tamil, the Father Language

tamil: ஐந் தலகுநிலையும் உபய கலைநிலையும் மூன்று மெய்நிலையும் அமைந்துள்ளதும், சம்புபக்ஷத்தாரால் அனாதியாய் - சுத்த சித்தாந்த ஆரிஷ ரீதிப்படி கடவுள் அருளாணையால் - கற்பிக்கப்பட்டதும், எப்பாஷைகளுக்கும் பிதுர்பாஷை யென்று ஆன்றோர்களால் கொண்டாடப்பட்டதும், இனிமை என்று நிருத்தம் சித்திக்கப்பெற்றுள்ளதுமான தமிழ் என்னும் இயற்கை உண்மைச் சிறப்பியல் மொழிக்குச் சுத்த சித்தாந்த பதஉரை:-
translation: Tamil holds the five units, the twofold state of the powers and the three consonants. It was taught from beginningless time by those of Sambhu's side (campupakṣattār; Sambhu is a name of Siva), by the command of God's grace, according to the way of the sages (āriṣa rīti) of Suddha Siddhanta. The noble ones have celebrated it as the father language (piturpāṣai) of all languages. By etymology (niruttam) its name has been established to mean sweetness. To this language called Tamil, the special language of natural truth, here is the Suddha Siddhanta commentary on its parts (pata-urai):
commentary: The introduction to the printed edition relates that the Sankaracharya of Vallalar's day, meeting him in Chennai, praised Sanskrit as the "mother language". Vallalar answered that Tamil, then, is the "father language", and wrote this commentary to show the wisdom of Tamil. Here he states his ground. Tamil was not made by human beings: those of God's own side taught it from beginningless time, by the command of His grace. The old Tamil lexicons give "sweetness" as a meaning of the word Tamil. Siddhānta means "established conclusion"; Suddha Siddhanta is the pure conclusion of the Saiva teaching. A pata-urai explains a word part by part: here t-a, m-i and ḻ.

sections.title: T and A: The Form of Siva and Arut Perum Jothi

tamil: த் - அ:- தத்வரூபாதி சிவபோகாந்தமான தசகாரிய இயற்கை உண்மைக் கட்டளை நிலையில், முன் அலகு நிலைப்பொருள் கூறியவிடத்துக் குறித்த ஏழாவது நிலையாகிய த் என்பது சிவரூப இயற்கையுண்மைக் கட்டளையாம். அ - அகண்டாகார சித்கலா ரூப ஓங்காரத் துட்பொருட் பிரதம விலக்கிய வியக்தி அக்கரம். பன்னீருயிர் நிலையிற்றலையாய முதலக்கர மாதலில், அதுவே பிரமாதி பரசிவாந்த நவநிலைக்கும் அனாதியாதி காரணமாயுள்ள இயற்கையுண்மைப் பரிபூரணப் பொருளிலக்காம். என்னவே, சிவரூபமாகும் தகராகாசத்தில் சுத்த சிவமாகும் அருட்ஜோதி யிணைந்துள்ள பூரணானந்த ஸ்வரூப பரபதி வியக்த மாயிற்று.
translation: T–a: There is an order of natural truth of the ten operations (tacakāriyam), running from the form of the tattvas to the enjoyment of Siva. In it, t, which was marked as standing in the seventh place when the meaning of the units was given above, is the stage of natural truth that is the form of Siva (Siva-rūpa).

A is the letter in which the inner meaning of Omkara, whose form is the undivided power of consciousness, is first indicated and made manifest. Since it is the first letter, the head of the twelve vowels (uyir), it is itself the mark (ilakku) of the all-full Reality of natural truth, which is the beginningless first cause of the nine stations from Brahma to Para-Siva.

So: in the small inner space of the heart (takarākācam), which is the form of Siva, Arut Perum Jothi, who is pure Sivam, abides united; and thus the Supreme Lord (parapati), whose own form is perfect bliss, has become manifest.
commentary: The Saiva teaching counts ten stages (tacakāriyam) in the soul's way: the form, vision and purification of the tattvas (the constituents of existence); the form, vision and purification of the soul; then the form, vision, union and enjoyment of Siva. The seventh is the form of Siva, and t is the seventh consonant. A, first of all letters, marks the Reality that is the first cause of the nine stations of the divine, from Brahma the creator up to Para-Siva. The letter t is called takaram in Tamil; takaram also names the small inner space of the heart. So t-a reads: in that inner space Arut Perum Jothi abides, and there the Lord of perfect bliss is revealed. He is met within, in the heart of the soul.

sections.title: M and I: The Support and the Soul

tamil: ம் - இ:- சங்கார ப்ரணவமாகிய மகாரம் முக்தான்மாக்களுக்கு ஒளிவண்ணச் சதானந்தமாயும் பெத்தான்மாக்களுக்கு இருள்வண்ண மலரூபமாயும் இருந்து கற்பாந்தப் பிரளய முடிவின் சிருஷ்டி திதியாதிகளில் சிதான்ம சக்தியாகிய ஜீவனுக்கு அதிகரணமாகவும், முற்குறித்த பத்தாவது நிலயமாகிய ஆன்மாதாரமாகியும் உள்ளதெனப் பொருளாம். இ - பன்னீருயிர்நிலைகளில் மூன்றாம்நிலை உயிராகிய இகாரம் திரிகலா ஆன்மவருக்கத்தில் அபரமாகிய சகலாகலரையும் பரமாகிய பிரளயாகலரையும் கீழ்ப்படுத்தி அவ்விரு கூட்டத்தாருக்கும் மேற்பட்டு நின்ற சுத்த விஞ்ஞானகலராகிய சிதாத்மாக்களைச் சுட்டுகின்றதாம். என்னவே, ஆதார ஆதேயக் கூட்டுறவால் என்றுந் தோன்றி விளங்கும் சிதான்ம வருக்கங்கள் பரபதி லக்ஷியமாகிய பூரணானந்தத்திற்கு அனுபவிகளாக உரியவர்களெனக் குறிக்கொள்ளல் வேண்டும்.
translation: M–i: The letter m (makāram), the pranava of withdrawal, is eternal bliss, the colour of light, to the liberated souls (muktāṉmākkaḷ), and the form of impurity (mala), the colour of darkness, to the bound souls (pettāṉmākkaḷ). At the end of the dissolution that closes an aeon, in creation, preservation and the rest, it is the ground (atikaraṇam) of the jīvaṉ, the power of the conscious soul; and it is the support of the soul, the tenth station marked above. That is its meaning.

I: The letter i, the vowel that stands third among the twelve vowels, points to the conscious souls, the pure Vijnanakalas (cutta viññāṉakalar). In the threefold class of souls, they stand above both other groups, the lower, the Sakalas (cakalākalar), and the higher, the Pralayakalas (piraḷayākalar), and keep them beneath.

So it must be noted that the classes of conscious souls, which appear and shine forever through the union of support and supported (ātāram and ātēyam), are entitled, as those who experience it, to the perfect bliss, the goal (lakṣiyam) that is the Supreme Lord.
commentary: The pranava Om holds a, u and m: creation, preservation and withdrawal. M is the withdrawing sound. The same reality is light and bliss to the freed soul and the darkness of impurity (mala) to the bound one: what differs is the soul's state. When the worlds begin again after each dissolution, m is the ground that holds the soul. The Saiva teaching grades souls by their impurities: the Sakalas are bound by three (āṇavam, the soul's innate darkness; karmam, deeds; māyai, the matter of bodies and worlds), the Pralayakalas by two, the Vijnanakalas by āṇavam alone. I points to the highest. Support (m) and supported (i) together say one thing: the Lord's perfect bliss is meant for souls, and they have the right to experience it.

sections.title: The Letter Zh

tamil: ழ்:- இந்தச் சிறப்பியல் அக்கரம் பதினெண் மெய்களில் பக்ஷமுடிபின் எண் குறிப்பில் நின்று, சிவயோக பூமியாகிய பரதகண்டத்தில் பௌராணிக தத்துவத்தாற் குறிக்கப்பட்ட ஐம்பத்தாறு தேசங்களுள் சுதேசந்தவிர மற்ற ஐம்பத்தைந்து தேச பாஷைகளிலும் இல்லாததாயும், பதினெண்ணிலமாகக் குறிக்கப்பட்ட செந்தமிழ் கொடுந்தமிழ் என்னும் இருமைக்கும் ஒற்றுமை யுரிமையாயும், முத்துறைத் தமிழுக்குள் முதன்மைத் துறையானதும் இருக்கு யஜுர் சாமம் என்னும் சமஸ்கிருத வேதத்திரயப் பொருள் அனுபவத்தை எளிதில் கற்றுணர்ந்து தெளிந்து அனுபவித்தற்குப் பரமேசுரனது திருவருளைப் பஞ்சாக்ஷர முத்தொழிற் காரியமான பஞ்சதசாக்கரியால் பிரத்தியக்ஷானுபவம் சித்திக்கச் செய்யும் நிலயமானதும், ஸ்ரீமாணிக்கவாசகர், சம்பந்தர், நாவரையர், சுந்தரர், திருமூலர் முதலிய மகாபுருஷர்களால் சாத்திர தோத்திரங்களாக அருளிச்செய்யப்பட் டிருக்கும் திருவாசகம், தேவாரம், திருமந்திரம் என்னும் பரமார்த்த ரகசியங்களை உடையதும், பலநாள் நைஷ்டிக அதிகரணம் பூண்டு போதகாசிரியர் சந்நிதியில் தாழ்ந்து சகபாடிகளோடு சூழ்ந்து சுர ஒலிபேதங்களைத் தேர்ந்து உழைப்பெடுத்து ஓதினாலும் பாடமாவதற்கு அருமையாயும், பாடமானாலும் பாஷியம், வியாக்கியானம், டீக்கா, டூக்கா, டிப்பணி முதலிய உரைகோள் கருவிகளைப் பொருள்கொள்ளத் தேட வேண்டியதாயும், அவ்வவைகளையும் தேடிக் கைவரினும் அக்கருவிகளால் போதகம் பெறவேண்டியதற்குப் பாஷியகாரர்கள் வியாக்கியானகர்த்தர்கள் டீக்காவல்லபர்கள் டூக்காசூசகர்கள் முதலிய போதக உபபோதக ஆசாரியர்கள் கிட்டுவது அருமையில் அருமையாயும் இருக்கிற ஆரியம் மகாராட்டிரம் ஆந்திரம் என்ற பற்பல பாஷைகளைப் போலாகாமல், பெரும்பாலும் கற்பதற்கு எண்ணளவு சுருக்கமாயும், ஒலி இலேசாயும், கூட்டென்னுஞ் சந்தி அதிசுலபமாயும், எழுதவும் கவிசெய்யவும் மிக நேர்மையாயும், அக்ஷர ஆரவாரம் சொல்லாடம்பரம் முதலிய பெண்மை அலங்கார மின்றி எப்பாஷையின் சந்தசுகளையும் தன் பாஷையுள் அடக்கி ஆளுகையால் ஆண்டன்மையைப் பொருந்தியதுமான தற்பாஷைக்கே அமைவுற்ற ழ், ற், ன் என்னும் முடிநடு அடி சிறப்பியல் அக்கரங்களில் முடிநிலை இன்பானுபவ சுத்த மோனா தீதத்தைச் சுட்டறச் சுட்டும் இயற்கை உண்மைத் தனித்தலைமைப் பெருமைச் சிறப்பியல் ஒலியாம்.
translation: Ḻ: This special letter stands among the eighteen consonants at the number that marks the end of a lunar fortnight (pakṣam). In Bharata Khanda, the land of Siva-yoga, the Puranic scheme (paurāṇika tattuvam) names fifty-six countries; ḻ is found in none of the languages of the fifty-five countries other than its own. It belongs in common to both Sentamil and Koduntamil, refined and regional Tamil, which are counted as the eighteen lands.

Its own language, to which alone the special letters ḻ, ṟ and ṉ belong, is the foremost branch of threefold Tamil (muttuṟait tamiḻ). It is the station where the holy grace of Parameswara becomes direct experience through the fifteen-letter mantra (pañcatacākkari), the working of the Panchakshara in its three functions, so that the meaning of the three Sanskrit Vedas, Rig, Yajur and Sama, may be learnt, understood, made clear and experienced with ease. It holds the supreme secrets of the highest truth, the Tiruvasagam, the Tevaram and the Tirumantiram, given in grace as scriptures and hymns by great souls such as Sri Manikkavasagar, Sambandar, Navaraiyar (Appar), Sundarar and Tirumular.

It is not like the many languages such as Āriyam (Sanskrit), Mahārāṣṭram (the language of Maharashtra) and Āndhram (Telugu). In them, even if one takes the vow of a lifelong celibate student (naiṣṭikam) for many days, bows low in the presence of the teacher, gathers round with fellow students, masters the differences of accent and sound and recites with toil, the text is hard to get by heart. Even when it is learnt by heart, one must search out the tools of commentary, great commentaries (pāṣiyam), expositions (viyākkiyāṉam), glosses (ṭīkkā, ṭūkkā), notes (ṭippaṇi) and the like, to grasp the meaning. Even when these are searched out and found, the teachers and assistant teachers through whom one must receive instruction by those tools, the authors of great commentaries, the makers of expositions, the masters of glosses, the explainers of ṭūkkā and the rest, are the rarest of the rare.

Tamil, for the most part, is small in the count of what must be learnt, light in sound, and very easy in its sandhi, the joining of sounds. It is very straightforward to write and to compose verse in. It has no feminine ornament, such as clamour of letters and pomp of words; and because it holds and rules within itself the metres of every language, it has a masculine nature.

Of the special letters ḻ, ṟ and ṉ, which belong to this language alone as its crown, middle and foot, ḻ stands at the crown. It is the special sound of the unique supreme greatness (taṉittalaimai) of natural truth, which points, until all pointing ends, to the pure state beyond silence (mōṉātītam), the crowning experience of bliss.
commentary: A lunar fortnight has fifteen days, so "the number that ends a fortnight" is fifteen: ḻ is the fifteenth consonant. Threefold Tamil is Tamil of literature, music and drama. The Panchakshara is the five-syllable mantra of Siva; working in three functions it becomes fifteen, the number of ḻ. Vallalar's verdict on Āriyam, Mahārāṣṭram and Āndhram is plain: hard to learn by heart even after long discipline, needing layers of commentary, with teachers "the rarest of the rare". Tamil is brief, light and direct. His image of "feminine ornament" against a "masculine nature" speaks of a language's sounds and decoration, the clamour of letters and pomp of words; it is no judgement on women. In the Great True Petition he says the same: God turned him from Āriyam to Tamil, easy to learn and sweet to sing. Ḻ, the crown of Tamil's own letters, points beyond all pointing to the bliss beyond silence.

sections.title: The Summary

tamil: உரை கூறிப்போந்த சுத்தசித்தாந்த ஆரிடரீதி முப்பதவுரைப் பொழிப்பு:- மருளியற்கை மல இருளைப் பரிபாகசத்தியால் அருளொளியாக்கி, அதற்குள்ளீடான சிதாத்ம சிற்கலாசத்தி என்னும் சுத்த ஆன்மாவானது, தகர, ககன, நடன அருட்பெருஞ்ஜோதி என்னுஞ் சுத்த சிவானந்த பூரணத்தை சுத்த மோனாதீத வியலால் அனுபவிக்கும் இயற்கை உண்மையே தமிழ் என்னும் சொற்பொருள் சுட்டினவாறு காண்க.
translation: The summary (poḻippu) of the commentary on the three parts, given above in the way of the sages of Suddha Siddhanta: The pure soul is the conscious power (ciṟkalācatti) of the conscious soul, which lay enclosed within the darkness of impurity, whose nature is delusion. By the power of ripening (paripāka catti) it turns that darkness into the light of grace; and, in the pure state beyond silence, it experiences the fullness of pure Siva-bliss called Arut Perum Jothi, of the inner space (takaram), of the vast expanse (kakaṉam) and of the dance (naṭaṉam). See that this natural truth is what the meaning of the word Tamil points to.
commentary: The three parts together tell the whole way. The soul lies enclosed in the darkness of impurity. As it ripens, that same darkness is made the light of grace, and the pure soul experiences the fullness of Siva's bliss: Arut Perum Jothi, who shines in the small space of the heart, in the boundless expanse and in the dance of grace. The experience lies beyond silence itself. This is the natural truth the word Tamil points to. Arut Perum Jothi is real, and every soul is made for this experience.

sections.title: The Meaning: Tamil Gives the Experience of Pure Sivam

tamil: இதன் கருத்து யாதெனில்:- தமிழ்ப்பாஷையே அதிசுலபமாகச் சுத்தசிவானுபூதியைக் கொடுக்கு மென்பதாம்.
translation: If it is asked what this means: it is that the Tamil language itself gives the experience of pure Sivam (cuttacivāṉupūti) most easily.
Thiru Chitrambalam.
commentary: Vallalar ends with the plain sense of the whole work. Cuttacivāṉupūti is the direct experience (anupūti) of pure Sivam, God free of every impurity. He says the Tamil language itself gives it, and gives it most easily. The reasons stand above: the word's own letters trace the soul's way to Arut Perum Jothi, its scriptures hold the secrets of that way, and the language asks no rare teachers or endless commentaries before it opens.

glossary.def: Syllable-unit of Tamil prosody: nēr (one syllable, short or long) or nirai (two syllables, the first short). The preface venba moves through forty of them, which Vallalar reads as the thirty-six tattvas and the strength of their three groups (Ozhivilodukkam §22).

The three faults of a definition or proof (Skt. asambhava, avyāpti, ativyāpti): impossibility (it fits nothing), too narrow (it misses cases it should cover) and too wide (it takes in cases it should not) (Ulagelam §13).

Ashrama: the four prescribed stages of life (student, householder, forest-dweller, renunciant), bound to varna. The Veda is bound by the measure of varna and ashrama and so is current only in part; the True Word is not bound by it (Ulagelam §14). See varuṇam.
The non-conscious: what is not the self and has no knowing of its own. In the worlds beyond the causal (Ulagelam, Part 2), each tattva is perceived as non-conscious before it is relinquished.
The impure state and the pure state of the soul. Vallalar reads gu in Gururayan as darkness, the impure state, and ru as grace, the pure state into which the guru lifts the soul (Ozhivilodukkam §8).
Support (Skt. ādhāra); in the yoga worlds of the Ulagelam, the centres of the body on which the yogi fixes attention. See ātāram, ātēyam.

Path (Skt. adhvan): the six orders into which Saiva teaching sorts all the worlds: letter (varṇa), word (pada), mantra, bhuvana, tattva and kalā. Part 2 of the Ulagelam counts all their worlds within Ulagelam.

The scriptures of temple worship, mantra and practice, chiefly of the Saiva tradition. In part they follow the Veda, and where they reject the doctrine of the one Self they oppose it. Since they mostly explain the effects of the two kinds of maya, Vallalar holds them authority, for the most part, for the word of Mahesvara, Sadasiva and the others, and no authority for the Turiya word (Ulagelam §15).

The sense of "I" (Skt. ahaṅkāra; also written āṅkāram in the Ulagelam), one of the tattvas: the inner instrument that takes each act as one's own. The words of men, gods and sages come from it, of low, middle and high quality (Ulagelam §3).
Oneness, union: what the guru's feet bring about when placed on the disciple's head in the initiation of wisdom (Ozhivilodukkam §12).
Of Indra; the Aindra liberations are the liberations of Indra's realm, among the tattvic worlds of the Ulagelam.
The five kings: the five sons of Pandu in the Mahabharata, Dharma (Yudhishthira) and his brothers.
The named bhuvanas (world-regions) of Part 2 of the Ulagelam, each the world of a presiding being, rising to the world of Sadasiva.
The "unspoken" prayer: the mantra that the breath repeats of itself, without the tongue. It is a limb of breath control and a yoga world of its own (Ulagelam, Part 2).
Pride, egoism; in verse it can appear as antai by loss of a middle syllable (Ozhivilodukkam, footnote 53).
Metonymy: a word that names something closely tied to its first meaning. Uḷḷam, "mind", names the knowing (pōtam) that rises within (Ozhivilodukkam §16).
"He of the Light without measure": a name of Siva in the opening verse of the Periya Puranam. Vallalar came to name this Light Arut Perum Jothi, the Supreme Light of Grace (Ulagelam §20).
Unit: here each of the five written sounds of the word Tamil, t-a-m-i-ḻ (Tamil §2).
Means of valid knowledge, means of proof (Skt. pramāṇa). Three are counted: perception (kāṭci), inference (karutal) and the testimony of the word (urai aḷavai) (Ulagelam §13, §14).

glossary.term: Ambika, Vama, Jyeshtha, Raudri, Jaya, Vijaya, Ajita, Aparajita
glossary.tamil: அம்பிகை, வாமை, சேட்டை, ரௌத்திரி, சயை, விசையை, அசிதை, அபராசிதை
glossary.def: Named powers, each with its world among the tattva worlds of the Ulagelam.
Non-otherness, not being other (Skt. ananya).
What is beyond bliss: the state past Siva-bliss, to which Sambandar holds the right and leads souls (Ozhivilodukkam §11).

The soul's innate darkness, the first of the three impurities (mala) of the Saiva teaching; the Ozhivilodukkam and the Tamil commentary write āṇavam. Vallalar also calls it the inborn, beginningless impurity (cakaca malam, Skt. sahaja mala); the Vijnanakalas are bound by it alone. Part 2 of the Ulagelam gives it a tattva world with the full run of thirty-four powers.
The language of Andhra, Telugu; named by Vallalar with Āriyam and Mahārāṣṭram as languages hard to learn and to understand (Tamil §8).
The soul tattvas (24) and the knowledge tattvas (7): with the five pure Nada tattvas, the three groups of the thirty-six tattvas in Saiva teaching (Ozhivilodukkam §22).
A compound that names something outside its own words, as "Bluebeard" names a man. "Ozhivilodukkam" as the name of a book is such a compound (Ozhivilodukkam §24).

Those who love: in Vallalar's reading, those who long unceasingly for Siva-bliss alone, not for wealth or fame. The book is for all of them, of any caste or religion, if they are ripe: ripeness decides, not caste or religion (Ozhivilodukkam §18).
The inner instrument: mind, intellect, cittam and the sense of "I" taken together, in which the soul forms notions and distinctions about what the senses bring (Ulagelam, Part 2).
Brahmins: here those who stood in the Hall of Grace at Chidambaram when the True Word was spoken (Ulagelam §12).
The soul, the "atom" of Saiva usage: the sense the root uḷ, "within", takes in uḷḷam (Ozhivilodukkam §16).
"It wastes as it is experienced"; glossed by Vallalar as running out while being experienced.
Direct experience, realisation (Skt. anubhūti). See cuttacivāṉupūti.
Lower, as against para, supreme. The True Word is not a matter of lower speech, so its grammar is not dissected (Ulagelam §8).

Lower knowledge or lower wisdom, the wisdom of words (vācaka ñāṉam) gained from study of scripture; and supreme knowledge or higher wisdom, the wisdom of experience (aṉupava ñāṉam), direct knowing of the Real. Vallalar holds that the author spoke from supreme knowledge, not book learning (Ozhivilodukkam §19).
Consecration (Skt. abhiṣeka); an apiṭēkap peyar is the name given at consecration into an order of teachers. Vallal was the author's consecration name (Ozhivilodukkam §4).
King. The king commanded Sekkizhar to compose the Periya Puranam; tradition names him Anapaya Chola (Ulagelam §10).
A sifter: one who sifts gold and the like out of rubbish heaps.
The way of the sages (Skt. ārṣa, "of the rishis"); Vallalar gives his commentary according to it.

Āriyam: Sanskrit. Vallalar's verdict is plain: with Mahārāṣṭram and Āndhram it is hard to learn by heart even after long discipline, and needs layers of commentary and rare teachers (Tamil §8). In the Great True Petition he says the same: God turned his desire from Āriyam to Tamil.
Appearing shrunken.

Arut Perum Jothi, the Supreme Light of Grace: Vallalar's ultimate name for God. In the Tamil commentary He is pure Sivam abiding in the small inner space of the heart, the fullness of Siva-bliss the pure soul experiences (Tamil §6); the Light without measure of the Periya Puranam is the One Vallalar came to name so (Ulagelam §20). The Jothi is God Himself, not a light God owns; it is real and open to every soul.
The Hall of Grace at Chidambaram; potu means what is common to all (Ulagelam §10).
Posture: the first limb of yoga in the Ulagelam's worlds of means and attainment. Forty-six postures are named before the world of liberation by yoga in its limb of posture.
Support and supported (Skt. ādhāra, ādheya): m is the support, i the soul it supports (Tamil §7). See adhara.
Line of verse; also foot. The venba's four lines are the four feet of wisdom: pure charya, kriya, yoga and jnana (Ozhivilodukkam §23).
Ground, substratum, the locus that holds a thing (Skt. adhikaraṇa). Not atikāraṇam (supra-causal).

The transcendent: what lies beyond (Skt. atīta, gone beyond). Sambandar stood to the ripe as hidden truth, to the very ripe as truth experienced, and beyond both as the truth beyond (Ozhivilodukkam §8). See Turiya.
The non-dual and the dual paths. The fallen disputants keep to neither (Ozhivilodukkam §10).

"That rises close" (of the honey): formed from two roots, aṭu, to cling close, and aṭukku, to pile layer on layer; so the honey of bliss is without gap in place or time and rises upon itself without end (Ozhivilodukkam §17).

State, condition (Skt. avasthā). In the Ozhivilodukkam, the changing states of the soul that overpower teachers who have only learned (Ozhivilodukkam §5), and from which the guru's feet guard those who have entered bliss (Ozhivilodukkam §13). In the Ulagelam, the five states, waking, dreaming, deep sleep, turiya and the transcendent, counted in the sakala, kevala and pure conditions, in bondage and in liberation.
Full of ignorance (Skt. avidyā, ignorance).
The illustration of iron: iron yields tools easily and hides its golden nature far away; so the Veda yields passing pleasures easily and hides its real teaching (Ulagelam §14).
The land of Bharata, India; called by Vallalar the land of Siva-yoga (Tamil §8).
A world-region, one of the six paths (adhvas): the dwelling places of the presiding beings, from Aja up to the world of Sadasiva. "World" in the translation is kept for ulaku.

The primal light, the seed-point from which sound and form unfold (Skt. bindu), paired with Nada; a pure tattva and a lord, which in Part 2 of the Ulagelam stands where the usual list of thirty-six tattvas has the Shakti tattva. The apara-bindu (lower Bindu) belongs to pure maya and is the source of the Pranava word; the para-bindu (supreme Bindu) belongs to Grace, and Vallalar calls the apara-bindu its power (Ulagelam §3, §6, §14).

Brahma is the creator god; his nine worlds open the tattvic worlds of the Ulagelam. Brahman is the Absolute of the Vedanta: "the soul is Brahman" is the view of one of the schools whose liberation Vallalar counts among the tattvic worlds.
The opening at the crown of the head, and the point twelve finger-breadths above it. With the navel, throat and forehead they are five centres in the Ulagelam's yoga worlds.
The intellect: the inner instrument of knowledge, which inquires and decides.
Conjunction (Skt. saṁyoga): the joining through which the Lord's five Powers work with prakriti, mohini and Bindu (Ulagelam, Part 2).
The Sakalas: souls bound by all three impurities (anava, karma and maya); the lowest of the three classes of souls (Tamil §7).

God with form and parts, and God formless (Skt. sakala, niṣkala). The Vedas and Agamas came from the first; Ulagelam from the formless in its fullness (pūraṇa niṣkaḷam), "unarndhothar kariyavan" from the formless in part (Ulagelam §16).
With qualities and beyond qualities (Skt. saguṇa, nirguṇa). The True Word has an aimed-at sense beyond qualities (Ulagelam §16, §18).
In classical poetry on outer life, the sub-theme praising the nobility of the noble; it belongs to vākai, the theme of excellence and victory (Ozhivilodukkam §21).

Universal harmony (Skt. sama, equal; rasa, essence): the first word of the full name of Vallalar's path, Samarasa Suddha Sanmarkkam. The dance of grace in the Chit Sabhai dances in all six ends as the direct realisation of this harmony (Ulagelam §9).
Those of Sambhu's side: the teachers who stand on the side of God (Sambhu, a name of Siva), by whom Tamil was taught from beginningless time.
Expiatory fasts: the lunar fast, in which food is increased and decreased with the moon, and a penance of hard fasting (Ulagelam §14).
Notion, intent (Skt. saṅkalpa); for Parai it is Siva's intent to give grace. Series: caṅkaṟpa vikaṟpam, "notions and distinctions".
Euphonic increment: a linking syllable placed between a word and its ending, such as -attu- in uḷḷattu. Vallalar reads it as a sign that the stirring of knowing needs a support (Ozhivilodukkam §16).
Means and attainment: the practice, and what it reaches. The fourth group of the Ulagelam's worlds is "the worlds of means and attainment in the pure tattvas".

The six ends (Skt. ṣaḍ-anta): Yoganta, Kalanta, Nadanta, Bodhanta, Vedanta and Siddhanta, the summits of six schools of practice and thought. The dance of the Chit Sabhai holds all six in harmony (Ulagelam §9); in the Great True Petition Vallalar calls the sects and paths bearing these names distinctions of attainment of a slight fraction of the Suddha Sanmarkkam experience.
The universe of sound and meaning (Skt. śabda-artha): words and what they name, arising together. It is impure, pure-impure, pure or Turiya, by the level of its cause (Ulagelam §6).
The shadow-man: the image of one's own shadow seen in the sky after gazing at the shadow and then at the sky.
The "speaking" rhythm proper to the venba; the preface verse has its flowing form (Ozhivilodukkam §22).
Setting to work; or bringing about action of bad character (Skt. ceṣṭā, activity).
The two model forms by which Tamil grammar names verbal participles (viṉaiyeccam): the ceytu type ("having done") and the ceya type ("to do", "as").

The four ways of Saiva practice: service (charya), worship (kriya), yoga and wisdom (jnana, ñāṉam), the highest; the Ozhivilodukkam is a book of wisdom (Ozhivilodukkam §20, §22). Each way holds the other three within it, which gives the sixteen stages charya-charya, charya-kriya … jnana-jnana, each with its worlds in Part 2 of the Ulagelam.

The Hall of Consciousness: the shrine at Chidambaram where Siva dances, and the space of pure consciousness it stands for. It is not one of the spaces produced by maya; it lies beyond Nada, and the True Word appeared there (Ulagelam §4, §9, §10).
A fetter (Vallalar's gloss vilaṅku).

A metrical foot, the measured unit of Tamil verse; the same word means excellence. The venba's fifteen feet match the fifteen subjects of the Ozhivilodukkam (Ozhivilodukkam §23), and God's phrase "Ulagelam unarndhothar kariyavan" has four of them (Ulagelam §21).
The special letters of Tamil, ḻ, ṟ and ṉ, which belong to Tamil alone.
Special letter: Vallalar's name for ḻ, the letter of special nature (Tamil §4).
The conscious power of the soul: the pure soul itself (Tamil §9).

Consciousness, and the power of consciousness (Skt. cit-śakti). When the power of consciousness alights on the para-bindu, Nada arises, and the Turiya word with it (Ulagelam §6, §13); with the power of bliss (āṉanta catti) it is the gateway through which the Siva-jnanis speak (Ulagelam §17).
The Space of Consciousness (Skt. cidākāśa): the name the Vedas and Agamas give the Chit Sabhai (Ulagelam §4).
The secret of Chidambaram (Skt. rahasya): the empty space in the shrine, the space of consciousness itself, which the Chit Sabhai signifies (Ulagelam §9).
The conscious soul.
Power of consciousness: what the vowels a and i stand for (Tamil §3).
The reflecting mind: one of the four inner instruments, with mind, intellect and the sense of "I".
Siva-wisdom: the wisdom whose nectar Sambandar drank at three, given by the Goddess as the Lord graced (Ozhivilodukkam §11).
The Siva-jnanis, sages of Siva-wisdom, who spoke from Nadanta with no ego, by Siva's freedom. Their words Vallalar accepts as authority for the True Word (Ulagelam §17).
Siva-bliss: the bliss of Sivam, the Auspicious, which rises like honey where the soul's stirring knowing has ceased; the honey of the preface verse (Ozhivilodukkam §3, §17).
A whirling firework, in Vallalar's day and region called cuḻalpuṟicu.
Inference by a similar example (Skt. sādharmya, sharing a property): here the wind, which rises outside and fills what is within (Ulagelam §13).

Freedom: the power to act by one's own right. What Siva begins in His freedom (civa cutantaram) the soul cannot complete by its own freedom (jīva cutantaram) (Ulagelam §11). The Siva-jnanis speak by Siva's freedom; the Vedas and Agamas were spoken from their speakers' own freedom (taṟcutantaram) (Ulagelam §17).
Pure awareness. The worlds beyond the causal are held in it at five depths: outer-outer, outer, inner-outer, inner and inner-inner.
The pure Vijnanakalas: souls bound by anava alone, the highest of the three classes of souls; the vowel i points to them (Tamil §7).
The experience of pure Sivam: the direct experience of God free of every impurity, which the Tamil language itself gives most easily (Tamil §10).

glossary.term: Dipika, Rochika, Mochika, Vyomarupa, Ananta, Anatha, Anasrita
glossary.tamil: தீபிகை, ரோசிகை, மோசிகை, வியோமரூபை, அநந்தை, அநாதை, அநாசிரிதை
glossary.def: Named powers, each with its world among the tattva worlds of the Ulagelam.

A participle (literally "remainder"); a peyareccam is one completed by a noun, as veṉṟa, "who won", is completed by "Sambandan". Eccam also means a young child, so the grammar shows Sambandar won as a boy (Ozhivilodukkam §11).
The doctrine of the one Self (Skt. ekātma): that all selves are one. Some Agamas argue against it and so oppose the Veda (Ulagelam §15).
In part, partial. The Veda, bound by varna and ashrama, is current only in part; "unarndhothar kariyavan" came from the formless in part (ēkatēca niṣkaḷam) (Ulagelam §14, §16).
Craving (Skt. eṣaṇā). The three cravings are for children, wealth and the world's regard; Indra has a world of them among the tattvic worlds.
Tamil rhyme on the second letter of each line (vaḷḷal, vaḷḷaṉ). The author's name stands at the head of the rhyme (Ozhivilodukkam §4, §12).
The Vedic prayer to the sun; one Prajapatya liberation is its experience.
The three qualities of prakriti, sattva, rajas and tamas. In Part 2 of the Ulagelam they form a tattva world of their own; "quality" in the lists renders kuṇa as an aspect.
A word the sense calls for but the text leaves out, for the hearer to supply: "Kannudaiya" before "Vallal" (Ozhivilodukkam §4).
Figurative use of a word beyond its literal sense (Skt. lakṣaṇā). "Debate" read figuratively means any contest, against birth, sickness or poison (Ozhivilodukkam §10).
Mark, target: what a sign points to. The letter a, first of the vowels, is the mark of the all-full Reality (Tamil §6). See lakṣiyam.

The coconut tree (editors' footnote in the modern prints; the 1932 edition glosses it as a palmyra): its fruit needs a hard climb and then a tool; so the Veda's teaching needs providence and then Vedantic inquiry (Ulagelam §14).
The king of the gods; his six worlds are among the tattvic worlds of the Ulagelam.

The Lord as ruler: one of the five pure tattvas, which impels pure-impure raga; also a lord of the pranava-atom worlds. The Vedas and Agamas are words of Isvara that appeared in the form with parts (Ulagelam §16).
Loss of a middle syllable, a change of form allowed in verse (e.g. akantai > antai).
Natural truth: truth that is God's own nature, not made and not received from anything else. Vallalar calls ḻ its special letter and Tamil its special language (Tamil §4).
Muttered prayer, fire-offering, a Vedic offering, and a Soma sacrifice: among the regular rites of the Veda (Ulagelam §14).
Power in which the inert (jaṭam) and consciousness are joined: what the consonants t, m and ḻ stand for, like a body that carries a soul (Tamil §2).
The inert: insentient matter, with no consciousness of its own (Skt. jaḍa; the Ozhivilodukkam writes caṭam). The author discerned that all the tattvas are inert (Ozhivilodukkam §3).

Compassion for all living beings, the foundation of spiritual life in Vallalar's teaching. In the Tamil commentary he grounds it in the consciousness every living being carries, which has never left the Lord (Tamil §3).
The conscious power of the individual soul: what the vowel i stands for.
The individual soul, a living being.
Light; in the yoga worlds of the Ulagelam, one of the objects on which the yogi fixes concentration. Vallalar's own name for God is Arut Perum Jothi, the Supreme Light of Grace.
The sky, the vast expanse; one of the three places where Arut Perum Jothi shines, with takaram and naṭaṉam.

(1) The tattva that removes a portion of the soul's darkness and lets it act. (2) The five kalās, Nivritti, Pratishtha, Vidya, Santi and Santyatita, the widest of the six paths (adhvas) by which Saiva teaching divides the worlds; four of them also name yoga worlds. See kalai.
A power or ray of a reality (Tamil §2); also art, as in Kalanta, the end of the arts (Ulagelam §9). See kalā.
A Tamil verse form of four lines, each of four feet. The opening verse of the Periya Puranam is written in it, and God's phrase fills its first line (Ulagelam §21).
Here read as the elixir medicines of the Tamil siddha tradition, by which some seek a liberation of the body. The word also means an aeon.
The paths of action, charya and the rest; the books that teach them sort people by caste, religion and custom, shutting some out, not by ripeness (Ozhivilodukkam §18).

Rites (Skt. karma): Vallalar lists the Veda's endless classes of them, regular (nitya), occasional (naimittika), for desired ends (kāmya), forbidden acts (niṣēdha), expiation (prāyaścitta) and worship (upāsanā) (Ulagelam §14). See karma.
The invocation: the verses of prayer that open a book or commentary.
A name given for a reason, for the meaning it carries: Vallal for the author, Gururayan for Sambandar (Ozhivilodukkam §4, §5).
Gripping hard with the teeth and gnawing.

Deeds and their fruits, the second of the three impurities; the Tamil commentary writes karmam. Part 2 of the Ulagelam gives it a tattva world of its own; there the word is "karma" wherever it names the soul's binding deeds, and elsewhere it is rendered "act".
The conduct of ritual action and the conduct of wisdom. The Ozhivilodukkam unfolds only the conduct of wisdom (Ozhivilodukkam §19).
Inference (Skt. anumāna), the second means of proof; it rests on pervasion (viyātti). By it Vallalar proves that the True Word was spoken both outside and within (Ulagelam §13).
Instrument: the tattvas and faculties, whose nature the author discerned along with his own and that of grace (Ozhivilodukkam §15).
A question.
Wailing; appears altered as kataṟṟal (Ozhivilodukkam, footnote 51).
An outer binding tied over something to hide it.
A small tinkling bell; kiṇkiṇi vāyceytalartal, to blossom with a round face like a little bell's mouth.
Teacher of ritual and teacher of wisdom. Kannudaiya Vallal was first a teacher of ritual, then of wisdom; Sambandar is the king of the teachers of wisdom (Ozhivilodukkam §3, §4).
The leafy top of the sugarcane.
A sheath: one of the coverings of the soul's body; the sheaths form a tattva world among the outer instruments (Ulagelam, Part 2).

Pure maya in its first stirring as Om, also called Kundali, pure maya coiled as potential. It is the common, inherent ground of the whole universe of word and meaning; Kundali also names a world of liberation by yoga (Ulagelam, Part 2).
Lesser lords: those holding lordship, known and honoured by a few.

The sense aimed at: what words point to beyond themselves (Skt. lakṣya, target). The Periya Puranam's expressed subject is the devotees; its aimed-at subject is divine grace (Ulagelam §2). See vācciyam.
The sign of Siva, worshipped as His form that is with form and formless; in the Ulagelam's lists, also the own form of the universes, bodies and souls.
The language of Maharashtra; named by Vallalar with Āriyam and Āndhram as languages hard to learn (Tamil §8).

The Great Lord, a form of Isvara; his worlds stand with Rudra's, Sadasiva's, Bindu's and Nada's among the worlds of the primal, eternal impellers. The Agamas are authority, for the most part, for the word of Mahesvara, as Ulagelam §15 spells it.
A great lord, known and honoured by many.
The letter m; in the pranava Om, the sound of withdrawal.

Impurity: what binds and darkens the soul; the Saiva teaching counts three, anava, karma and maya. The same reality is light and bliss to the freed soul and the darkness of impurity to the bound one (Tamil §7).
The mind: the inner instrument of desire, whose notions and distinctions rest on the objects it wants.
The radiance of a smile (Skt. mandahāsa, a gentle smile).
Sacred formula and sacred diagram. The mantra is also one of the six paths (adhvas); both name worlds of liberation and Saiva schools in Part 2 of the Ulagelam.
A firework.
Making a horse of palmyra stems and mounting it; in classical Tamil love poetry, the public act of a man refused by the woman he loves.

The matter of bodies and worlds, the third of the three impurities (Tamil māyai). Part 2 of the Ulagelam names its kinds: root maya (mūlamāyā), mohini, impure maya, pure-impure maya (cuttācutta māyai, the source of the word of Rudra and the others), pure maya and yoga maya. All spaces formed from maya, even pure maya, are effects and pass away (Ulagelam §3, §4).
Body; in grammar, a consonant: a consonant cannot sound without a vowel, as a body cannot live without the soul.

The True Word: a word spoken by God, not made by any person. Opened with a case relation it means "the word that has truth" (the Pranava word, true in the expressed sense); opened without one, "the word that is truth" (the Turiya word of Grace, true in the sense aimed at) (Ulagelam §5, §6).
The deluding maya, from which kalā and the limiting tattvas arise; a conjunction (caiyōkam) through which the Lord's Powers work (Ulagelam, Part 2).
Silence: the words of the Siva-jnanis are full of it (Ulagelam §17).
The state beyond silence (mōṉam, silence; atītam, gone beyond): the pure state in which the soul experiences Siva-bliss, to which the sound ḻ points (Tamil §8).
Liberated souls and bound souls (Tamil §7).
Root maya: the effect of mohini and the material cause of the impure tattvas the soul enjoys (Ulagelam, Part 2).
A deity in embodied form (Skt. mūrti, form): in the Ulagelam, the divine form arising from Bindu, before which charya and kriya are done.
Glossed by Vallalar word by word: muṭi, the head; kaḷacam, removal; mutti, liberation.
Threefold Tamil: Tamil of literature, music and drama.
The falling sickness, epilepsy, from which Sambandar freed the daughter of the Mazhavan (Ozhivilodukkam §10).

Sound, the subtle primal sound in which all speech begins (Skt. nāda; nātam in the Ozhivilodukkam's word list), paired with Bindu; the highest of the pure tattvas, standing where the usual list has the Siva tattva. Nadanta, the end of Nada, is where all sound has come to rest; the Siva-jnanis speak from there, and the Chit Sabhai lies beyond Nada (Ulagelam §4, §6, §17).
A channel of the vital breath in the body; the ten nadis are joined in breath control, and the nadis form a tattva world (Ulagelam, Part 2).
The vow of a lifelong celibate student who lives with his teacher.
Nakedness (Skt. nagna).
The earthworm (nākappūcci).
A word of the print in the Ulagelam's yoga worlds (the five-, eight-, ten-, twelve- and sixteen-naṭa Bindu centres); its sense is uncertain.
The dance: God's dance of grace; one of the three places where Arut Perum Jothi shines.
The knower, knowing and the known (Skt. jñātṛ, jñāna, jñeya), glossed by Vallalar as the one who sees, the seeing and what is seen.
The standard line of four feet, holding ten to fourteen letters, bare consonants not counted (Tolkappiyam, Seyyuliyal 38) (Ozhivilodukkam §23).
The four-line venba whose second line ends in a detached word (taṉiccol) that rhymes with the third. The preface verse is one (Ozhivilodukkam §1).
A heap of paddy not yet winnowed.
Stainlessness (Skt. nirmala): the nature of a book of pure wisdom, shown by the bare, unadorned words of the verse (Ozhivilodukkam §19).
A stage above Bindu in the Ulagelam's yoga worlds, printed so; probably the stage called nirodhikā.
Etymology (Skt. nirukta): by it the name Tamil is established to mean sweetness.
Order, restriction: the tattva that binds each soul to the fruits of its own deeds.

The sacred syllable Om, which the Tamil commentary counts as five letters: a, u, m, bindu and nāda. The Pranava word of Sadasiva comes from the apara-bindu and is true only in the expressed sense (Ulagelam §3, §5, §6). Kudilai has the nature of Omkara, and the pranava-atoms of Part 2 of the Ulagelam are its forms, the bodies of Rudra, Isvara, Sadasiva, Shakti and Siva.
"Having discerned": discerning by sinking into a thing until its nature stands clear, and staying clear without wavering (Ozhivilodukkam §15, §19).
Kannudaiya Vallal's classic of spiritual wisdom: oḻivu, cessation, and oṭukkam, subsiding: the stillness of the self where its stirring has ceased. Vallalar printed it in 1851.
Bondage (Skt. pāśa, noose, fetter): what binds the soul (pacu). Sambandar's "victory in debate" stands for victory over bondage, the sign of wisdom (Ozhivilodukkam §20).
The soul and the Lord: two of the fifteen subjects of the Ozhivilodukkam, with bondage (Ozhivilodukkam §23). In the Tamil commentary Pati, the Lord, is what the vowel a stands for (Tamil §3).
The bound state of the soul, which the experience of bliss takes away as food takes away hunger (Ozhivilodukkam §18).
Turning a bag inside out from its mouth so that its contents come out.
A mock play: an outward disguise showing what is not as though it were; or a comic play.
The subject of an inference (Skt. pakṣa): the thing about which something is proved; the mark must be present in it (Ulagelam §13).
The ripe: souls ready to receive grace; atipakkuvar, the very ripe (Ozhivilodukkam §5, §8). God has given them teachings and other holy words, never an incomplete word (Ulagelam §11).
Many holes (pal + tuḷai).
A lunar fortnight of fifteen days; "the number that ends a fortnight" is fifteen, the place of ḻ.
The fifteen-letter mantra: the Panchakshara working in its three functions.
The five-syllable mantra of Siva.

The supreme Power of the Lord (Skt. parā śakti), the supreme power of grace. With the primal Power and the powers of desire, knowledge and action, she is one of the Lord's five Powers, and has her own world in Part 2 of the Ulagelam; the Ozhivilodukkam makes known the vision of Parai and union with her.
The Supreme Lord, whose own form is perfect bliss.
The power of ripening, by which the darkness of impurity becomes the light of grace (Tamil §9).
Perfect fullness, wanting nothing.
Than, compared with.
The tools of commentary on Sanskrit texts: great commentaries, expositions, glosses and notes.
Film, veil: a film over the eye, as in cataract. The tattvas lay over the soul's sight (āṉma tiruṭṭi) like it, until the inner word removed it from Sekkizhar (Ulagelam §12).
Commentary on the parts of a word: here on t-a, m-i and ḻ.
Names of yoga postures (the lotus, the cow's face, the peacock, the cock …). Forty-six are listed before the world of liberation by yoga in its limb of posture (Ulagelam, Part 2).
A Vedic sacrifice for a desired end, listed with the horse sacrifice and the royal consecration (Ulagelam §14).
The Puranic scheme, which counts fifty-six countries in Bharata Khanda (Tamil §8).
Contemplation, devotion held in the mind. Vallalar rejects reading "placing on his head" as contemplation only: it was a real initiation (Ozhivilodukkam §14).
A dance danced circling from right to left.
Predicate: the part of a sentence that says what the subject is or does. "Ulagelam" alone has none, so it cannot be a complete word of God (Ulagelam §11).
Preface; a special preface speaks of one book and shows eight things: author, line, boundary, title, form, subject, hearers and benefit (Ozhivilodukkam §2, §24).
"The holy child": in the Ozhivilodukkam commentary, the name for Thirugnanasambandar, the guru of Kannudaiya Vallal.
The Pralayakalas: souls bound by two impurities, anava and karma, having shed the third; Vallalar names Brahma and the others among them.

Authority, valid proof (Skt. pramāṇa). The Vedas are authority for the words of men, gods, sages, Hari-Brahma and Rudra, the Agamas for those of Mahesvara and Sadasiva; neither is authority for the Turiya word (Ulagelam §14, §15).
Instruction in the Supreme (Skt. brahmopadeśa).
A reflected image (Skt. pratiphalita).
Setting to work, impelling (Skt. preraka).
To babble: Vallalar's word for his own explanation, made out of love (Ulagelam §18).
Father language: Tamil, celebrated by the noble ones as the father language of all languages (Tamil §5).
Summary: the gathered sense of a commentary.

Knowing, awareness. In the Ozhivilodukkam, the soul's own knowing, the sense "I know", stirred by latent impressions (vātaṉai); when it ceases (pōta oḻivu), the honey of Siva-bliss rises (Ozhivilodukkam §3, §16, §17). Bodhanta is the end of knowing (Ulagelam §9).
Of Prajapati, the lord of creatures; the Prajapatya liberations are among the tattvic worlds of the Ulagelam.

Primal nature, primal matter (Skt. prakṛti; also written pirakiruti): the source of the gunas and of the bodily tattvas; the series renders the Tamil pakuti "primal matter". The word of Hari (Vishnu) and Brahma comes from it (Ulagelam §3), and in Part 2 the Lord's Powers act in conjunction with prakriti, mohini and Bindu.
A word printed in all three editions of the Ulagelam ("grace in the prakti form"); its sense is uncertain, possibly vyakti, "manifest", or a short form of pirakiruti.
The vital air; "prana and the other vital airs" form a tattva world (Ulagelam, Part 2).

Breath control, withdrawal of the senses, concentration, meditation and absorption: the limbs of yoga after posture. Each has its world of liberation in Part 2 of the Ulagelam, preceded by a list of its own parts.
The karma that has already begun to bear fruit in the present life (Skt. prārabdha). One tattvic liberation aims at its destruction, and it is the aim of the Karma Saiva school.
Union without merging: as ru and rā meet in Gururayan without fusing, Sambandar's bliss was joined with his human form without being changed by it (Ozhivilodukkam §8).
The outer instruments: the senses and organs of action, purified in Sekkizhar by hearing the outer word (Ulagelam §12).
The soul as the experiencer of maya, joined to kalā and the other limiting tattvas.
Attachment, desire for enjoyment: one of the limiting tattvas. The print of the Ulagelam uses two forms of the word in the same run, arākam and then rākam.
Breathing out, breathing in and holding the breath: parts of breath control.

A form of Siva. His four worlds (Rudra, Pranava-Rudra, Upa-Rudra, Pratyanga-Rudra) open the worlds of the primal, eternal impellers, and the same pattern follows for Mahesvara, Sadasiva, Bindu and Nada. The word of Rudra and the others comes from pure-impure maya (Ulagelam §3).
Being-Consciousness-Bliss: the nature of the Real experienced in undivided oneness with Siva.
The pure tattva of Sadasiva's form, which impels impure prakriti.

A form of Siva, Lord of the pure order; his world closes the list of bhuvanas, and his worlds stand among the worlds of the primal, eternal impellers. His Pranava word comes from the apara-bindu (Ulagelam §3).
The first of the five faces of Siva and their mantras (Sadyojata, Vamadeva, Aghora, Tatpurusha, Isana); it begins the worlds of the mantra path in the Ulagelam.

Of Siva. The Saiva schools (Suddha, Asuddha, Misra, Siddhanta, Pasupata, Vama, Bhairava, Kalamukha, Mahavrata and others) each have their own world of liberation among the Ulagelam's worlds of means and attainment in the pure tattvas.

Two states of the soul in Saiva teaching: in sakala the soul is joined to body and instruments and to all three impurities; in kevala it lies alone with its darkness (anava). With the pure state (cuttāvattai) they make the three conditions in which the Ulagelam counts waking, dreaming, deep sleep, turiya and the transcendent, in bondage and in liberation.
The school that explains the world by two principles, prakriti and purusha; its liberation is counted among the tattvic worlds.
The six modes of being (Skt. ṣaḍbhāva): the six changes of all that exists, birth, existence, growth, change, decline and death.
Refined (literary) Tamil and regional Tamil.

Power (Skt. śakti; Tamil catti), in this volume usually rendered "power": the working capacity of a tattva, such as its power of form, of pervading or of arising, each counted as a world of its own in Part 2 of the Ulagelam. "Shakti" names Siva's own Power as a tattva and a lord.

"The settled conclusion": the name of the Saiva Siddhanta schools, whose liberations the Ulagelam counts among the worlds of means and attainment. The Ozhivilodukkam holds Siddhanta and Vedanta as one path (Ozhivilodukkam §22); the Petitions place Siddhanta among the paths that are distinctions of attainment of a slight fraction of the Suddha Sanmarkkam experience.
Attainment, accomplishment (Skt. siddhi): the eight attainments such as becoming minute, vast, heavy and light (aṇimā, mahimā, garimā, laghimā), which the Ulagelam counts among the yoga worlds.

God as pure being, free of every impurity; the Tamil commentary speaks of pure Sivam. The supreme Siva (paracivam) is His highest state, and the worlds of the Ulagelam end in oneness with Siva and in what lies beyond its joy.
The form of Siva: the seventh of the ten stages (tacakāriyam).
The aggregates of Buddhist teaching; one tattvic liberation of the Ulagelam is read as "aiming at the destruction of the aggregates".
"I am He": the contemplation by which the soul identifies itself with God; it names liberations among the tattvic worlds and the worlds of means and attainment.
The pure Siddhanta: the pure "established conclusion" of the Saiva teaching; Vallalar gives the Tamil commentary in its way and its technical language (Tamil §1, §5).
The ten stages of the soul's way: the form, vision and purification of the tattvas; the form, vision and purification of the soul; the form, vision, union and enjoyment of Siva.
The small inner space of the heart (Skt. dahara ākāśa), which is the form of Siva and where Arut Perum Jothi abides (Tamil §6).
The name of the letter t; also the small inner space of the heart, one of the three places where Arut Perum Jothi shines.
Foot; also effort, bolt and clasp. The guru's feet bring the soul into bliss, bolt it safe there and clasp it to Siva (Ozhivilodukkam §13).
The link between one metrical foot and the next; Tamil prosody counts seven kinds, of which the venba uses two (Ozhivilodukkam §22, §23).
The detached word ending the second line of a nēricai veṇpā (Ozhivilodukkam §23).
Unique supremacy: lordship that stands alone (taṉi, single, without a second).
The subtle elements, sound, touch, visible form, taste and smell, from which the gross elements arise.

The constituent principles (plural tattvas) of which bodies, senses, minds and worlds are made; Saiva teaching counts thirty-six. The author of the Ozhivilodukkam discerned them to be inert and passed beyond them (Ozhivilodukkam §3); their film dimmed Sekkizhar's soul-sight until the inner word removed it (Ulagelam §12), and Part 2 of the Ulagelam numbers 103 tattva worlds.
Derived from the tattvas. The tattvic worlds of the Ulagelam are worlds of gods and of the liberations held by the schools, which Vallalar counts as attainments that stay within the tattvas.
Water cleared with the clearing nut (tēṟṟāṅkoṭṭai, seed of Strychnos potatorum).

The holy small hall: the hall of the sacred dance at Chidambaram, also read as cit-ambalam, the hall of consciousness. It stands at the head of each work of this volume and closes Part 1 of the Ulagelam and the Tamil commentary.

Initiation (Skt. dīkṣā) by which a guru frees the disciple: ñāṉatīkkai, initiation into wisdom; tiruvaṭit tīkkai, initiation by the holy feet placed on the disciple's head (Ozhivilodukkam §5, §12, §14). The Ulagelam writes diksha: nirvana initiation, the highest Saiva initiation, is held to subdue karma and the six paths.
The veiling power: the Lord's beginningless, eternal Power that works to aid the ripening of the soul's karma.
The holy closing verse of a hymn of the Thevaram; by one word of his, Sambandar made the male palmyra female (Ozhivilodukkam §9).
The power of divine grace, the first cause of bounty, which the holy feet are (Ozhivilodukkam §12).

Compounded and uncompounded: words fused into a compound with the link dropped, or standing open in a phrase (Ozhivilodukkam §4). Tokai uvamai, a compressed simile, as "flower-feet" (Ozhivilodukkam §13).
Sound-linkage binding a verse, such as rhyme and alliteration; orūut toṭai, the spaced linkage (Ozhivilodukkam §23).

The real teacher (Skt. sadguru). The Lord's power of desire reaches souls as the true Guru, whose form is knowledge, appearing with form (Ulagelam, Part 2); in a former birth Sambandar, as Kumara Satguru, was the true Guru who taught Haran and Agastya (Ozhivilodukkam §6).
Glossed by Vallalar as tumpu aviḻttu, "having untied the tether".

"The fourth": the state beyond waking, dreaming and deep sleep; beyond it lies the transcendent state (atītam). "The para-bindu Turiya word of Grace" is Vallalar's name for the True Word (Ulagelam §3).
The raised, unraised and sounded accents of Vedic chant (Ulagelam §14).

"All the worlds" (also written Ulagelam): the first word of the Periya Puranam, given by God to Sekkizhar in the Hall of Grace at Chidambaram, opening the line "Ulagelam unarndhothar kariyavan", "He whom all the worlds find hard to know and to tell" (Ulagelam §1, §2). Part 2 unfolds its meaning as five groups of worlds.
Devotion, worshipful meditation on God; the Misra Saiva liberation aims at devotion that holds the Veda and the Agama equal.

The testimony of the word: knowledge from a trusted source, the third means of proof. Vallalar will not take it from the Vedas and Agamas for this Word, but takes it from the Siva-jnanis (Ulagelam §14, §17).
Three rites of purification that open the list of the parts of breath control in the Ulagelam's yoga worlds.

The highest true path: the head of the four paths of Saiva teaching (of the servant, the son, the friend, and the true path, Sanmarkkam), to which the author of the Ozhivilodukkam belongs (Ozhivilodukkam §4).
Life, the soul; in grammar, a vowel.
The expressed sense: what words plainly say (Skt. vācya). Paired with lakṣiyam, the sense aimed at (Ulagelam §2, §5, §6).
Here, the word that says with right reason, "Do this," "Give this up."
Of the Veda; the Vaidika Saiva Siddhanta liberations are counted among the Ulagelam's worlds of means and attainment.

The four levels of speech in Saiva teaching: the spoken word, the word formed within, the word as a seen intent, and its subtlest seed; all ordinary speech is their effect (Ulagelam §6). The Ozhivilodukkam's word list defines subtle speech (cūkkumai vākku) as a power standing at the navel as sound, the first cause of words; Part 2 of the Ulagelam names the four Vaikhari, Madhyama, Pasyanti and Sukshma.
The poetic theme of excellence and victory (Ozhivilodukkam §21).

The bountiful giver; the name of the author, Kannudaiya Vallal, and the epithet of Sambandar's feet. Bounty is unfailing grace, virtue, steadiness, freedom from craving and anger, and unceasing love, giving to each as each needs (Ozhivilodukkam §4, §12).
Bounty: a word of many meanings (giving, virtue, fame, beauty, abundance), the first part of vaḷḷal (Ozhivilodukkam §4).
The letter, the word and the "braided" recitation: special parts of the Vedic text (Ulagelam §14).

Varna: the fourfold division of people by birth into castes (brahmin, kshatriya, vaishya, shudra). The Veda is bound by the measure of varna and ashrama, does not let people of all castes and religions alike recite and understand it, and so is current only in part; the True Word is not bound by it and is current everywhere (Ulagelam §14). In the Petitions Vallalar calls caste custom false worldly custom.

Latent impressions (Skt. vāsanā): the traces past experience leaves in the soul, which stir up its knowing (pōtam) (Ozhivilodukkam §3, §16). The Ulagelam writes vācaṉā: in its highest worlds only these remain to be relinquished.
Debate, contest; read figuratively, any contest that grips a soul (Ozhivilodukkam §9, §10).

Case relation and non-case relation: the two ways Tamil grammar opens a compound. With a case relation a case ending is understood ("word having truth"); without one the first part names what the second is ("word that is truth") (Ulagelam §5). In the Ozhivilodukkam, Gururayan is joined through the fourth case, the dative (Ozhivilodukkam §7).
Empty renouncers: those who look as if they have let go only because they have nothing to enjoy.
Letting go (Skt. visarjana).
Limited knowledge: the tattva that lets the soul know a little. Pure vidya (cuttavittai) is the first of the five pure tattvas, which impels pure-impure vidya.
Silence (mauṉam).
A change of a word's form, allowed in verse (kataṟal > kataṟṟal, Ozhivilodukkam, footnote 51).
An incomplete verb; literally "a lessening of action (karma)". Ōrntu, "having discerned", stands last to show that karma lessens for those who learn the book (Ozhivilodukkam §19).
A detailed commentary (Skt. vṛtti), such as Vallalar's on the preface verse of the Ozhivilodukkam (Ozhivilodukkam §1).
The god Vishnu; his worlds (viṇṭulaku), including those that take a tattva for the self, are among the tattvic worlds of the Ulagelam.
Sense-pleasure, the pleasure of objects, which appears while the knowing self stirs; set against Siva-bliss (Ozhivilodukkam §13, §17).
Sounding without stopping in the middle.
The bliss of liberation, which Sambandar promised to those who worship his feet (Ozhivilodukkam §12).

What pervades and what is pervaded (Skt. vyāpaka, vyāpti): in the Ozhivilodukkam's word list, Vallalar glosses them as mingling and what is mingled with. In the Ulagelam, viyātti is pervasion, the constant tie between a mark and what it proves, as smoke goes with fire, on which inference rests (Ulagelam §13).
Stages beyond Nada in the ascent of yoga; each names a world of liberation by yoga in the Ulagelam.
Form, line (of teaching) and boundary: three of the eight parts of a special preface (Ozhivilodukkam §24).
